Issued at 1235 PM CDT Wed Oct 21 2026

THIS AFTERNOON: An absolutely beautiful mid-October afternoon 
is unfolding as winds have remain light, skies remain clear, and
temperatures are rising into the 70s. Dew points are mixing 
down into the middle 40s in a few areas, which could be a sign 
for later tonight. 

TONIGHT: A bit of high lvl cirrus that crosses the CWA later this 
afternoon and early evening will prevent a sharp temperature drop-
off initially.  However nearly all guidance is indicating that we'll 
see a night with light to calm winds and clear skies.  Given these 
conditions, will lower temperatures significantly in most locations, 
with HRRR/RAP guidance indicating potential for mid-40s.  With 
afternoon dew points likely falling a bit further, this leaves cross-
over temperatures in a favorable position to lead to fog 
development. The majority of this fog may be confined to sheltered 
river/valley areas, but given temperature falls, some may spill out 
into a broader area and become locally dense. 

THURSDAY: Troughing sliding into the Central Rockies will help 
intensify the SPG throughout the Plains on Thursday. Winds will 
begin to increase early in the morning and by the afternoon we'll 
see routine gusts 20 to 30 mph at times. Slowly drying fuels and 
increasing wind will lead to increased fire danger. See separate 
discussion for further details. 

FRIDAY:  Late Thursday night we'll begin to see an increase in low-
lvl moisture emanating from the Oklahoma Panhandle. This 
moisture, when combined with convergence on a 40 knot LLJ and 
weak dPVA, may lead to isolated to scattered high based showers 
after 3am Friday which will continue lifting northward Friday 
morning. A minor increase in elevated instability could lead to 
isolated lightning strikes with this activity. However, the 
greater threat in the afternoon and evening will be the surging 
high temperatures and increasing wind gusts. Latest guidance 
strongly supports sustained winds 20 mph in many locations, with
potential for gusts of 45 mph at times. While the SE surface 
wind direction is a bit mis-aligned with the strongest corridor 
of low-lvl SWLY flow, the highest wind corridor is likely to 
fall along and west of a Brookings to Yankton line. This will 
again increase fire danger so please read separate discussion 
for further details. 

SATURDAY-WEDNESDAY:  A warm overnight is anticipated into Saturday 
as the SPG really doesn't weaken and promotes increased mixing 
through the night.  By Saturday morning, a cold front will slowly 
slide east into Central South Dakota. Weak low-lvl convergence and 
moisture streaming ahead of this front could lead to high based 
showers into daybreak. A splitting upper trough over the Rockies 
will promote two distinct features, a progressive trough lifting 
northeast into southern Canada Saturday into Sunday, with a cutoff 
area of energy stalling over the Four Corners.  The aforementioned 
frontal boundary will get nudged southeast on Saturday, bisecting 
the CWA. With significant cold air lagging this front, the 
temperature gradient is not expected to be extreme.  However an 
increase in cloud cover, along with potential for occasional light 
rain will persist through Saturday and into Saturday night. 

One or more weak impulses traveling northeast along the stalled 
front will keep clouds and occasional rain risks through the CWA 
Saturday night and through Sunday. QPF amounts through Sunday 
afternoon may be on the lighter side, with most areas seeing less 
than 0.25".

That earlier mentioned upper low over the Four Corners begins to 
eject northeast by the end of the weekend and into Monday. A strong 
low-lvl frontal zone is expected to develop across the CWA ahead of 
this system, promoting increasing rain chances. The very slow 
northward movement of the approaching SW trough will keep high rain 
chances through the CWA on Monday and will likely continue into 
early Tuesday.   Latest NBM probabilities suggest high rain 
probabilities at near 100% for >0.10", potential for >0.50" near 70%-
80%, probabilities for >1.0" as high as 50% and probabilities 
for 2.0" totals at 20%. 

The passage of this system, and then the cooler air that follows it, 
will promote a return of more typical mid-late October temperatures. 
High temperatures Sunday through Wednesday are favored to be in the 
upper 40s to mid 50s.
